The Loading Bay
A practice brief for Action: an original scene written for SLATE, taped to a reader off camera.
The Loading Bay
The Safe Behind The Ring

A night-shift guard who has just been knocked down by an intruder has twenty seconds to get the keys back before the shutter closes on her colleague.

THE SCENE
Where And When
A distribution warehouse at three in the morning. The intruder took the shutter keys off her belt in the struggle; her colleague is pinned behind a fallen pallet on the far side, and the shutter is coming down on its timer.
The Two Of You
Strangers: she has never seen the intruder before, and he wants only to get out with the keys.
You Play
Dana, a security guard in her second month, winded and on her knees.
The Reader Plays
The intruder, backing toward the shutter with the keys.
How They Play It
Steady: playing opposite it asks nothing more than the scene does.
The Genre Asks
Command Of The Frame: Status and threat carried in the body and the look more than the words: the person everyone in the room watches. A self-tape in it is judged more on connection and execution, and calls on your presence and physical expression. Rehearsing on your feet: status is found standing, in how little you need to move.
Suspense Held: A threat kept alive under every line: what’s at stake never dropped, even in the quiet. A self-tape in it is judged more on consistency and interpretation, and calls on your focus and listening and responsiveness. The breakdown, then rehearsal: suspense is held by knowing at every moment what your character fears will happen, and keeping it alive through the scene.
Its chases and fights are staged techniques; between them the scenes turn on who holds the frame and what the threat is. The research found nothing on how it’s played, so this is estimated from its conventions.
What You Want
Get the keys back before the shutter reaches the floor.
What’s In The Way
He is bigger, he has the keys, and every second she spends talking the shutter drops another foot.
WHERE IT TURNS
She gets up and tries reason: he can leave, she only needs the keys. (Grave)
He refuses; she closes the distance, and the fight is two moves: his arm goes wide off frame and the keys drop at her feet. (Grave)
Keys in hand, she drops to her knees at the gap under the shutter, calling her colleague’s name as it lands. (Grave and Lyric, held at once)

1 change of tone between beats and 1 beat held two ways. Rehearsal is complete at 50% in a beat, up to 15% more in a beat a change leads into, and 8% more in one held two ways. Reason, then force, then relief at having the keys, held together with fear as the shutter lands.

WHAT THE LOADING BAY ASKS
Everyday Speech, on camera
Timing: Much. Every line races the falling shutter, so each beat has to land to the second.
Physical Work: Built On It. The scene is a struggle staged to the shutter’s timer: the getting up, the two moves, the drop to the gap.
Playing Off The Partner: Much. What she tries depends on what he does with the keys.
Vocal Demand: Some
Tone: grave to lyric, 1 transition to play. Reason, then force, then relief at having the keys, held together with fear as the shutter lands.
Techniques It Asks: Stage Combat. The two moves are a staged fight. Mark them solo at reduced speed against the reader’s called cues from off camera, with no contact and the keys on your side of the frame, so they repeat exactly on every take.

Last Launch From The Roof
A practice brief for Anime: an original scene written for SLATE, recorded alone at a microphone.
Last Launch From The Roof
The Spillway Walk

Dubbing an existing scene, an apprentice glider pilot tells her rival on the academy roof that she’s leaving tomorrow, and the lines have to fit mouths already drawn.

THE SCENE
Where And When
A dubbing booth. On the screen, a flight academy’s rooftop at sunset, gliders tied down in a rising wind; the animation is finished and every line must land on the lip movements already in it. In the story, she has just failed her final flight and has been sent home.
The Two Of You
Rivals since their first day, who have never once admitted they’re friends.
You Play
Haru, an apprentice pilot of seventeen, who laughs when she’s about to cry.
You Speak To
Rin, her rival, already recorded on the track. Play against his lines in your headphones.
The Genre Asks
Played Large: Feeling worn on the outside and sized to fill the frame: the voice and the body carry it as much as the face. A self-tape in it is judged more on execution and connection, and calls on your vocal expression, physical expression and presence. Rehearsing on your feet: a size the body and the voice can carry has to be found aloud and standing.
Dense Text, Exact: A lot of words, or difficult ones, delivered fluently and at speed: jargon, argument or deduction as second nature. A self-tape in it is judged more on execution and interpretation, and calls on your memory and focus. Learning the lines: fluency at speed is the lines learned past knowing them.
Dubbing asks for emotional truth sized to the drawn image while the timing fits mouth movements that already exist. This comes from the genre’s research, mostly held with low confidence.
What You Want
Say goodbye without letting him see it matters.
What’s In The Way
He won’t accept it, and every line has to fit a mouth that opens and closes on the picture’s timing, not hers.
WHERE IT TURNS
She jokes about the failed landing, fitting each quip to the drawn laugh. (Comic)
He says she’s the best pilot in the year, and her answer comes out too fast for the drawn mouth, so she has to find it again. (Comic and Grave, held at once)
She admits she wanted to fly against him forever, as the drawn sun goes down. (Lyric)

2 changes of tone between beats and 1 beat held two ways. Rehearsal is complete at 50% in a beat, up to 15% more in a beat a change leads into, and 8% more in one held two ways. Bravado, a crack she has to fit back into the picture, then the plain admission.

WHAT LAST LAUNCH FROM THE ROOF ASKS
Everyday Speech
Timing: Built On It. Every line fits mouth movements that already exist, so where each word falls is fixed by the picture.
Playing Off The Partner: Some
Vocal Demand: Much. The laugh that turns to tears is carried by the voice alone, and the volume rises with the wind on the track.
Tone: comic to grave to lyric, 2 transitions to play. Bravado, a crack she has to fit back into the picture, then the plain admission.
Techniques It Asks: Voice-Over. It’s a dub: you record alone at a microphone, in sync with the finished animation and his recorded lines.
It Only Takes: Set. The animation is finished, so every line has to land where the drawn lips already move. It can only be played set, the same way every time.

High Wind
A practice brief for Animated: an original scene written for SLATE, recorded alone at a microphone.
High Wind
The Lamp On Gull Rock

A paper kite who has always bragged about how high he flies has to talk the girl holding his string into letting him go before the storm drags her off the hill.

THE SCENE
Where And When
A grassy hilltop in a gale, as the storm comes in off the sea. The kite has climbed higher than ever, the string is cutting the girl’s hands, and she won’t let go because he’s her only kite. You record it alone in a booth before any of it is drawn.
The Two Of You
Best friends in the way a kite and its flyer are: she made him from a newspaper and a broken umbrella last spring.
You Play
Flap, the kite, small, boastful and much braver than he sounds.
You Speak To
Pell, the eight-year-old holding the string far below. She isn’t in the booth with you, so play to her as if she were.
The Genre Asks
Played Large: Feeling worn on the outside and sized to fill the frame: the voice and the body carry it as much as the face. A self-tape in it is judged more on execution and connection, and calls on your vocal expression, physical expression and presence. Rehearsing on your feet: a size the body and the voice can carry has to be found aloud and standing.
The actor puts a full physical performance into a voice alone, often before the picture exists. This comes from the genre’s research, mostly held with low confidence.
What You Want
Make her let go of the string.
What’s In The Way
She loves him, she’s stubborn, and he can only reach her with his voice over the wind.
WHERE IT TURNS
He crows about the height, the clouds, the gulls below him. (Comic)
A gust snaps him sideways and the boasting cracks into fright, still trying to sound fine. (Comic and Grave, held at once)
He tells her to let go, gently, and promises he’ll see the whole sea for her. (Lyric)

2 changes of tone between beats and 1 beat held two ways. Rehearsal is complete at 50% in a beat, up to 15% more in a beat a change leads into, and 8% more in one held two ways. Bragging, a fright he tries to hide behind the bragging, then a goodbye that’s quiet in a gale.

WHAT HIGH WIND ASKS
Everyday Speech
Timing: Some
Playing Off The Partner: Some
Vocal Demand: Built On It. The kite has no body on the day: the height, the wind and the courage are all in the voice.
Tone: comic to grave to lyric, 2 transitions to play. Bragging, a fright he tries to hide behind the bragging, then a goodbye that’s quiet in a gale.
Techniques It Asks: Voice-Over. You record alone at a microphone before the animation exists, so the whole performance, the gusts and the struggle included, has to be in what’s heard.

Closing Day
A practice brief for Docufiction: an original scene written for SLATE, taped to a reader off camera.
Closing Day
The Claim Ticket

On its last day of trading, the owner of a corner shop serves one regular customer, with an outline in place of a script and every line found in the moment.

THE SCENE
Where And When
A small corner shop on its last afternoon. The shelves are half empty, and the owner is selling off what’s left at cost. The camera watches as a documentary would. There are no written lines: you and the reader have the outline below and play it as the people would.
The Two Of You
Shopkeeper and regular. He has come in every day for fourteen years for the same paper and the same mints.
You Play
The shop owner, played close to yourself, at the end of thirty years behind the counter.
The Reader Plays
The regular customer, improvising too.
How They Play It
Steady: playing opposite it asks nothing more than the scene does.
The Genre Asks
Caught Live: Behavior that looks unrehearsed: real listening, the next line taken from what the other person just did. A self-tape in it is judged more on connection and responsiveness, and calls on your listening and responsiveness and adaptability. Rehearsing on your feet: what looks unrehearsed is found by playing it through until nothing is set but the wants.
Its main characters are often non-professionals playing themselves, unscripted, with genuine reactions. This comes from the genre’s research, mostly held with low confidence.
What You Want
Get through the last sale without making it a goodbye.
What’s In The Way
He wants it to be one, and he’s brought something with him.
WHERE IT TURNS
The usual sale: paper, mints, change, comments on the weather. (Comic)
He asks what she’ll do now, and she has no answer ready. (Grave)
He gives her what he brought, and she has to take it on camera, with no line prepared. (Grave and Lyric, held at once)

2 changes of tone between beats and 1 beat held two ways. Rehearsal is complete at 50% in a beat, up to 15% more in a beat a change leads into, and 8% more in one held two ways. An ordinary sale, a question with no answer ready, then a gift taken without a line.

WHAT CLOSING DAY ASKS
Everyday Speech, on camera
Timing: Some
Playing Off The Partner: Built On It. Every line is found from what the reader says, so the scene exists only between the two of them.
Freedom To Improvise: Built On It. There’s no script: the dialogue is improvised from the outline, the way real people would talk.
Tone: comic to grave to lyric, 2 transitions to play. An ordinary sale, a question with no answer ready, then a gift taken without a line.
Techniques It Asks: Improvisation. You improvise the scene to an outline, playing close to yourself the way a docufiction participant does.
It Only Takes: Open. The brief gives an outline and no lines, so there’s no set text to fix. It can only be played open, found fresh from the reader each time.

text:
Letters From The Lock
A practice brief for Documentary: an original scene written for SLATE, recorded alone at a microphone.
Letters From The Lock
Scratch Narration

A voice reads a canal lock-keeper’s wife’s letters to her sister, as narration under a documentary’s archive footage.

THE SCENE
Where And When
A recording booth. The documentary is about a canal that closed in 1923, and the letters, written for SLATE as an invented woman’s, are read over footage of the locks and barges. You read three letters, from 1911, 1915 and 1923. The footage under each is already cut, and each letter has to fit its length.
The Two Of You
Sisters who wrote every month for twelve years and met twice in that time.
You Play
The voice of Clara Hesketh, the lock-keeper’s wife, from her twenties to her thirties.
You Speak To
Her sister, the one person each letter is written to, though the documentary’s audience hears them over the footage.
The Genre Asks
Played Straight: Meant completely: the feeling played with full conviction, never winked at, however large or strange the material. A self-tape in it is judged more on believability and connection, and calls on your emotional depth and presence. The breakdown and the lines: believing it starts with knowing exactly what your character wants and why it matters to them.
Actors in documentaries read letters and narration: plain and meant, never performed at the audience. The research found nothing on how it’s played, so this is estimated from its conventions.
What You Want
Read the letters so the audience hears a woman writing to her sister, and only then a documentary’s narration.
What’s In The Way
There’s no picture of her and no one to play off, the footage dictates the timing, and the letters have to age twelve years in three minutes.
WHERE IT TURNS
1911: newly married, describing the lock and the barge families with wit. (Comic and Lyric, held at once)
1915: her husband has enlisted, and she runs the lock alone; the letter is all practical news, with the worry under it. (Grave)
1923: the canal is closing, and she tells her sister they’re leaving the cottage. (Grave and Lyric, held at once)

2 changes of tone between beats and 2 beats held two ways. Rehearsal is complete at 50% in a beat, up to 15% more in a beat a change leads into, and 8% more in one held two ways. A witty young letter, a wartime one with worry under the news, then a last letter that’s a goodbye to the place.

A widow visits her late husband’s business partner, each suspecting the other, and uses an embrace to find out whether he has the key to the deposit box.

Where And When

Bonnie, twenty-four, a waitress at the truck stop.

A hotel switchboard operator who listened in on a call she shouldn’t have finds the caller at her counter, and gives her account of the night afterward in her own words.

Where And When
The front desk of a downtown hotel in 1948, a little after two in the morning. An hour ago she connected a call from room 610 and stayed on the line long enough to hear a man arrange a death. Level One, Again
Dialogue Option Three

A fifty-two-year-old payroll clerk wakes in another world in the body of a nine-year-old shepherd, and talks her way through the status panel only she can see.

THE SCENE
Where And When
A hillside pasture in another world, at dawn. Last night she fell asleep at her desk during year-end payroll; this morning she woke in a stranger’s small body, in a field of sheep with two tails each, with a glowing panel of numbers hanging in the air in front of her. The villagers will come up the hill for their shepherd within the hour.
The Two Of You
The panel is the only thing here that speaks her language, and it answers in cheerful, useless messages.
You Play
Dolores Whitcomb, fifty-two, a payroll clerk with thirty years’ experience, now speaking with a nine-year-old’s voice.
You Speak To
The floating status panel only she can see. No one answers aloud: you read its messages and react to them.
The Genre Asks
Played Large: Feeling worn on the outside and sized to fill the frame: the voice and the body carry it as much as the face. A self-tape in it is judged more on execution and connection, and calls on your vocal expression, physical expression and presence. Rehearsing on your feet: a size the body and the voice can carry has to be found aloud and standing.
Belief In What Isn’t There: An invented world made concrete: the creature, the machine or the magic played as specifically as a cup of tea. A self-tape in it is judged more on believability and interpretation, and calls on your imagination. The breakdown: the world’s rules have to be worked out before they can be believed.
A voice actor plays a modern adult’s interior life inside a fantastical new body. This comes from the genre’s research, mostly held with low confidence.
What You Want
Work out the rules of this world before the villagers come for her.
What’s In The Way
The panel answers every question with a cheerful note about her progress, and nothing she knows seems to apply here.
WHERE IT TURNS

The Petition For Vengeance
A practice brief for Jidaigeki: an original scene written for SLATE, taped to a reader off camera.
The Petition For Vengeance
The Small Door In The Ward Gate

In the Edo period a samurai’s widow petitions the domain magistrate for a license to avenge her husband, and when he doubts she could carry it out, she shows him.

THE SCENE
Where And When
The magistrate’s audience hall in a castle town of the Edo period, on a winter morning. A vendetta then had to be licensed and registered, or the avenger was a common murderer. Her husband was killed in a quarrel four months ago, and the man who killed him has fled the domain. You Play
Kajiwara Fumi, twenty-nine, a samurai’s widow with a son of six, whose father taught her the sword as a girl.
The Reader Plays

How They Play It
Steady: playing opposite it asks nothing more than the scene does.
The Genre Asks

A self-tape in it is judged more on execution and interpretation, and calls on your physical expression, discipline and vocal expression. The breakdown and rehearsal together: the manners are researched first, then made habit on your feet.
Played Large: Feeling worn on the outside and sized to fill the frame: the voice and the body carry it as much as the face. A self-tape in it is judged more on execution and connection, and calls on your vocal expression, physical expression and presence. Rehearsing on your feet: a size the body and the voice can carry has to be found aloud and standing.
A contrived, formal, archaic register of speech, stock makeup and stylized fights. This comes from the genre’s research, mostly held with low confidence.
What You Want

What’s In The Way
He holds that a widow owes her house its heir before its honor, and every refusal comes in a courtesy she has to match.

Where And When
A community-center gym after the evening class, the mats still out. Three weeks ago she broke a man’s nose outside a bar; the coach agreed to one round, no audience, to decide whether she returns.
The Two Of You

A resident at the end of a night shift hands over a patient she’s worried about to an attending who thinks the numbers look fine.

Where And When
A ward corridor at seven in the morning, outside bed fourteen. The patient, a retired bus driver admitted with abdominal pain, has had a slowly rising heart rate and falling blood pressure through the night, each reading still short of the level that would trigger a call.
The Two Of You

You Play

The Last Pool
A practice brief for Nature Documentary: an original scene written for SLATE, recorded alone at a microphone.
The Last Pool
The Haypile

A narrator voices a sequence about a heron hunting in the last pool of a drying river at the end of a summer without rain.

THE SCENE
Where And When
A recording booth. The sequence is already cut: dawn over a cracked riverbed, a heron working one shrinking pool, the fish crowding, and at the end the first drops of rain. The narration script is written to the picture, with each line timed to a shot.
The Two Of You
The narrator speaks to a viewer watching at home, as a guide who has been there and wants them to see it.
You Play
The narrator, telling the story of the pool over the pictures.
You Speak To
The viewer at home, watching the sequence. Speak to them alone, as if no one else were listening.
The Genre Asks
Played Straight: Meant completely: the feeling played with full conviction, never winked at, however large or strange the material. A self-tape in it is judged more on believability and connection, and calls on your emotional depth and presence. The breakdown and the lines: believing it starts with knowing exactly what your character wants and why it matters to them.
A presenter’s voice-over and on-camera work: plain, warm and meant. This comes from the genre’s research, mostly held with low confidence.
What You Want
Carry the viewer through the sequence so they feel the dry season end.
What’s In The Way
The lines are fixed to the shots, and the story has to live inside the time each picture allows.
WHERE IT TURNS
Dawn on the riverbed: the scale of the drought, said quietly. (Lyric)
The heron misses three strikes in a row, and the narration lets the viewer smile. (Comic)
The fish crowd the last of the water; the narration says plainly what will happen if the rain doesn’t come. (Grave)
The first drops hit the pool. (Lyric)

3 changes of tone between beats and 0 beats held two ways. Rehearsal is complete at 50% in a beat, up to 15% more in a beat a change leads into, and 8% more in one held two ways. Quiet wonder, a gentle joke at the heron’s expense, the hard fact of the drought, then relief.

WHAT THE LAST POOL ASKS

The Culvert

A field medic drags a wounded enemy conscript into a drainage culvert under shellfire, and has to keep her sidearm from him and win his trust before she can save his life.

THE SCENE
Where And When
A concrete culvert under a road, in an invented war between invented countries, late afternoon. Shells are landing in the field above. She pulled him in because he was bleeding and closest. He woke up in the dark and saw her uniform.
The Two Of You
Enemies by uniform who share no language; he’s eighteen and she’s old enough to be his mother.
You Play
Corporal Ana Lisboa, forty-one, a medic for three years, tired past fear.
The Reader Plays
The conscript, eighteen, wounded in the leg and terrified, who speaks a language she doesn’t.
How They Play It
Steady: playing opposite it asks nothing more than the scene does.
The Genre Asks
States At The Limit: Fear, grief or exhaustion at their extreme, sustained, and believed though the threat is often not in the room. A self-tape in it is judged more on believability and execution, and calls on your emotional depth and physical expression. The lines, then rehearsal on your feet: an extreme state has to be found in the body, on lines you no longer think about.
Played Between Two: The scene lives between the two of you: chemistry, contrast, a part each that only works against the other. A self-tape in it is judged more on connection and responsiveness, and calls on your presence, listening and responsiveness and emotional depth. Rehearsing on your feet: a partnership is built in the exchange, played through until each part answers the other.
Boot camps so casts can play soldiers credibly, as a unit under fire. This comes from the genre’s research, mostly held with low confidence.
What You Want
Stop the bleeding in his leg before it kills him.
What’s In The Way
He thinks she means to kill him, and he’s reaching for her sidearm.
WHERE IT TURNS
She drops into cover breathless from dragging him the last few feet, and talks to him where he lies just off frame. (Grave)

The Teahouse Oath
A practice brief for Wuxia: an original scene written for SLATE, taped to a reader off camera.
The Teahouse Oath
Learned Through The Shutters

A swordswoman bound by an oath to her dead master is challenged at a teahouse by her sworn brother, who wants her to break it and avenge him.

THE SCENE
Where And When
An empty roadside teahouse in the mountains, an invented country in an earlier age, at dusk. Their master was killed by a rival school a month ago. Before he died he made her swear she wouldn’t avenge him. Her sworn brother has tracked her here.
The Two Of You
Sworn brother and sister, trained together for fifteen years under the same master.
You Play
Lan Yue, thirty, the master’s best student, who has kept her oath through a month of shame.
The Reader Plays
Wei Shan, her sworn brother, who thinks her oath is cowardice.
How They Play It
Steady: playing opposite it asks nothing more than the scene does.
The Genre Asks
Command Of The Frame: Status and threat carried in the body and the look more than the words: the person everyone in the room watches. A self-tape in it is judged more on connection and execution, and calls on your presence and physical expression. Rehearsing on your feet: status is found standing, in how little you need to move.
The World’s Own Logic: A world with rules of its own, absurd, dreamlike or satirical, played wholeheartedly by them and never commented on. A self-tape in it is judged more on interpretation and execution, and calls on your imagination and physical expression. The breakdown: the world’s logic has to be found before it can be played as if it were sense.
Wire- and trampoline-assisted acrobatics and sword action, bound by a chivalric code. This comes from the genre’s research, mostly held with low confidence.
What You Want
Keep her oath and keep her brother.
What’s In The Way
He draws on her to force the issue, and she won’t draw her sword against him.
WHERE IT TURNS
She pours him tea with full courtesy and tells him what the master asked. (Lyric and Grave, held at once)
He draws; she meets him with her sword still in its scabbard, three exchanges across the room marked solo to his called cues. (Grave)
His blade goes wide off frame; she lowers her sheathed sword, holds it across both palms and bows to him. (Lyric)

2 changes of tone between beats and 1 beat held two ways. Rehearsal is complete at 50% in a beat, up to 15% more in a beat a change leads into, and 8% more in one held two ways. Courtesy, a fight she refuses to win by drawing, then honor shown in a bow where a blow could have been.

Physical Work: Built On It. She fights three exchanges with her sword still sheathed, then lowers it across her palms in a formal bow, with control and grace.
Playing Off The Partner: Much. She answers his attacks and his accusations, never starting either.
Vocal Demand: Some
